Precocious

/prih-KOH-shuhs/ - the stress falls on KOH · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Precocious means advanced or developing far ahead of one's age.

By seven she had a precocious ear for languages, ordering the family's dinner in passable Portuguese after a week abroad.

Worked Example

The science-fair judges assumed the seismograph was a kit until its eleven-year-old builder showed the judges the spring she had wound herself, the pendulum she had re-tuned after the first quake read low, and the fix she had borrowed from a 1930s engineering paper. Precocious was the word every judge wrote, because the work was not good for eleven — it was good, and eleven.

Precocious is the exact word because it names development advanced far ahead of one's age — the calendar says child, the performance says otherwise. The Latin root means 'ripened early,' and the word keeps that image: fruit sweet ahead of the harvest. It praises timing as much as talent, and it belongs to the young; past a certain age, early ripening is just ripeness.

How Precocious Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

early-blooming

early-blooming: arriving at full flower ahead of the calendar

forward

forward: an older word for a child ahead of their years, now sounding dated

Antonyms

late-blooming

late-blooming: developing on a delayed schedule

immature

immature: not yet developed for one's age — the reverse complaint

How Strong Is It? — quick → precocious → prodigy-level

quick vs. precocious

quick vs. precocious: A quick student picks things up fast for any age; precocious means performing years beyond your age.

prodigy-level vs. precocious

prodigy-level vs. precocious: Prodigy-level goes past precocious — not just ahead of other children, but astonishing even among grown masters.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — pre-

Prefix — pre-: before

Root — coc

Root — coc: to cook, to ripen (Latin coquere)

Suffix — -ious

Suffix — -ious: full of, tending to

Put it together

Put it together: Pre- (before) + coc (to cook, to ripen) + -ious = ripened before its time. Latin praecox described fruit that sweetened ahead of the season, and Rome was already applying it to startling children. The kitchen is still in the word: precocious talent has finished cooking while everyone else's is barely warm.

Use the root in a new word: biscuit

Use the root in a new word: biscuit: Ship's biscuit was baked hard on purpose, made to survive months in a sailor's tin.

Word Choice

neutral, admiring (sometimes wry)

Precocious praises development ahead of one's age, and it belongs to the young — applied to adults it turns ironic. Its mirror in this unit is embryonic: an embryonic talent is barely formed, a precocious one has arrived early. For skill without any claim about age, gifted does the plainer work.
